## Ten of twelve labels are correct. Is that good enough? {.question-slide}

<div class="major-question">
What would you need to know before answering?
</div>

::: {.notes}
Do not reveal the downstream support-rate estimate yet. Collect criteria: prevalence, type of error, subgroup, inferential target, cost, human benchmark.
:::

---

## Four different jobs hide inside “coding text”

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Classification</strong> Assign a category</div>
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Extraction</strong> Retrieve a field</div>
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Measurement</strong> Represent a construct</div>
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Inference</strong> Support a claim beyond the coded cases</div>
:::
::::

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 42px;">A structured output completes the first two jobs—not automatically the last two.</div>

<div class="source-line">Barrie, Argyle, Bisbee et al., 2026 · “AI and Research Methods,” §10.2</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: Annotation produces categorical or numerical variables for downstream analysis and requires validation matched to use | Source: course chapter §§10.2.1–10.2.5 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

---

## The readings relocate the methodological burden

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<div class="kicker">Stuhler, Dang Ton & Ollion</div>

The model makes custom information extraction accessible.

**Burden:** articulate the tacit codebook, expose the promptbook, and study patterned error.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
<div class="kicker">Chae & Davidson</div>

Several training regimes can make classification effective.

**Burden:** choose among scale, examples, fine-tuning, task complexity, and cost.
:::
::::

<div class="source-line">Stuhler et al., 2025 · Chae & Davidson, 2026 · *Sociological Methods & Research*</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: Promptbooks make custom information-extraction tasks accessible while exposing non-random error | Source: https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251336794 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
- Claim: Chae and Davidson compare ten models and four training regimes for stance classification | Source: https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251325243 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

## A promptbook must state what humans often leave tacit

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
<div class="label human">Codebook</div>

- construct definition
- valid categories
- inclusion and exclusion rules
- edge cases
- human examples
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<div class="label model">Promptbook adds</div>

- exact message text and order
- output schema and missing-value rule
- model/runtime and parameters
- formatting and parsing instructions
- preserved prompts and outputs
:::
::::

<div class="semantic-line" style="margin-top: 34px;">Writing the promptbook can reveal that the original measure was underspecified.</div>

<div class="source-line">Stuhler, Dang Ton & Ollion, 2025 · DOI 10.1177/00491241251336794</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: Prompts require greater explicitness than many practical human codebooks and add formatting instructions | Source: https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251336794 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

## One obituary corpus contains several different task types

| Variable | What the system must do | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| Age | Find a usually explicit number | Formulaic and early |
| Military service | Search for a sparse fact | Needle in a haystack |
| Education | Apply categories and limited inference | Sparse + interpretive |
| Occupation | Summarize emphasized work | Distributed + semantic |

<div class="semantic-line validation" style="margin-top: 24px;">The correct method can vary within one dataset because the variables pose different information problems.</div>

<div class="source-line">Stuhler, Dang Ton & Ollion, 2025 · Obituary information-extraction study</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: The obituary project codes twelve variables with task properties ranging from direct extraction to sparse search and summarization | Source: https://oscarstuhler.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Stuhler_Ton_Ollion_ArXiv_preprint.pdf, Table 1 and discussion | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

---

## Larger generative models help most when the signal is sparse

| Variable | Llama 70B | Llama 8B | Conventional baseline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Gender · macro F1 | .92 | .79 | .99 |
| Military · macro F1 | .98 | .75 | .72 |
| Education · macro F1 | .78 | .40 | .29 |
| Age · accuracy | .99 | .99 | .95 |
| Cause of death · accuracy | .97 | .96 | .76 |

<div class="caption">Selected averages across prompting scenarios; baseline type differs by variable.</div>
<div class="source-line">Stuhler, Dang Ton & Ollion, 2025 · Table 7</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Data: Selected values from Table 7 comparing 70B/8B generative models with Longformer, Naive Bayes, or regex baselines | Source: https://oscarstuhler.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Stuhler_Ton_Ollion_ArXiv_preprint.pdf | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
Emphasize that the last column is not one common model. The point is task-method fit, not a model leaderboard.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="43%"}
<div class="evidence-number">.95</div>
<div class="evidence-label">accuracy from extracting the first plausible two- or three-digit number</div>
:::
::: {.column width="12%"}
<div style="font-size: 58px; margin-top: 72px; text-align: center;">≈</div>
:::
::: {.column width="43%"}
<div class="evidence-number">.99</div>
<div class="evidence-label">accuracy from the 70B and 8B generative models</div>
:::

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 34px;">An LLM is not automatically the most defensible tool just because it can perform the task.</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: A simple first-number regex achieves .95 age accuracy versus .99 for both generative models | Source: https://oscarstuhler.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Stuhler_Ton_Ollion_ArXiv_preprint.pdf, Table 7 and p. 30 discussion | Accessed: 2026-08-18

## Aggregate accuracy does not make error random

> Errors correlated with identity, time, text form, or a theoretical variable can bias the analysis that uses the labels.

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 54px;">The validation sample must reveal *which cases* fail—not merely how many.</div>

<div class="source-line">Stuhler, Dang Ton & Ollion, 2025 · Barrie, Argyle, Bisbee et al., 2026</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: Non-random prediction error can bias downstream estimates even when aggregate accuracy is high | Source: https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251336794 and course chapter §10.2.5 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

---

## Chae and Davidson vary more than model size

<div class="comparison-band"><strong>10 models</strong> tens of millions → hundreds of billions of parameters</div>
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>4 regimes</strong> zero-shot · few-shot · fine-tuning · instruction-tuning</div>
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Task</strong> stance toward a target—not generic positive or negative sentiment</div>

<div class="source-line">Chae & Davidson, 2026 · DOI 10.1177/00491241251325243</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Study design: ten models and four training regimes applied to stance classification | Source: https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251325243 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

---

## “Best model” is a decision about evidence and resources

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
<div class="label model">Large prompted model</div>

- strong performance with few or no examples
- low setup burden
- recurring API cost and version dependence
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
<div class="label human">Smaller fine-tuned model</div>

- requires labeled training data and compute
- can remain competitive
- lower inference cost and greater control
:::
::::

<div class="semantic-line" style="margin-top: 34px;">Choose for the exact task and inferential threshold—not for general benchmark prestige.</div>

<div class="source-line">Chae & Davidson, 2026 · Barrie, Argyle, Bisbee et al., 2026</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: The largest models generally perform best with little training data, while smaller fine-tuned models can be competitive and cheaper | Source: https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251325243 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
- Claim: Researchers should empirically compare cost and performance for their exact task | Source: course chapter §10.2.3 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

<div class="object-view">“I want lower rents, but I cannot support this proposal
unless the affordability rules become much stronger.”</div>

:::: {.columns style="margin-top: 38px;"}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<div class="label">Issue sentiment</div>

Positive toward lower rents
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
<div class="label failure">Proposal stance</div>

Conditional—no unqualified support
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: Stance detection identifies attitude toward a target and should not be collapsed into generic sentiment | Source: https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251325243 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
The excerpt is synthetic course material.

## Our toy corpus contains twelve synthetic public comments

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
<div class="object-type">list[dict]</div>
<div class="object-view">{
  "id": 3,
  "speaker_role": "renter",
  "text": "I want lower rents, but…",
  "human_label": "UNCLEAR"
}</div>
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
<div class="kicker">Inferential target</div>

Estimate the share of speakers who **explicitly support** the rezoning proposal.

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 34px;">Conditional approval is not explicit support.</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
All comments and labels are synthetic course materials. Ask what a list contributes and what each dictionary represents.

## The codebook is a Python dictionary before it is a prompt

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-8"}
CODEBOOK = {
    "SUPPORT": "explicit, unqualified endorsement",
    "OPPOSE": "explicit rejection or vote against",
    "UNCLEAR": "no stance, mixed, or conditional only",
}

valid_labels = list(CODEBOOK.keys())
```

<div class="semantic-line validation" style="margin-top: 26px;">Input: one dictionary → transformation: request its keys → output: one list of valid labels.</div>

::: {.notes}
Ask students to predict `type(CODEBOOK)`, `type(valid_labels)`, and the order/content of the list.
:::

---

## Messages separate stable measurement rules from each case

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-10"}
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_RULES},
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": f"Classify this comment: {comment['text']}",
    },
]

print(type(messages), type(messages[0]))
```

<div class="semantic-line" style="margin-top: 24px;">The API receives a list. Each message inside it is a dictionary.</div>

::: {.notes}
Ask a student to point to the string inside the nested structure. Explain that message roles are part of the recorded input, not invisible chat magic.
:::

---

## The hosted call is one replaceable transformation

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-9"}
from openrouter import OpenRouter

with OpenRouter(api_key=os.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY")) as client:
    response = client.chat.send(
        model=COURSE_MODEL,
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0,
    )
raw_text = response.choices[0].message.content
```

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 24px;">The required exercise uses cached output. No key is needed to inspect, parse, or validate it.</div>

<div class="source-line">OpenRouter Python SDK documentation · checked August 18, 2026</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Code syntax: Official OpenRouter Python SDK, `OpenRouter` client and `client.chat.send` | Source: https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/python/overview | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
Do not run the live call unless demonstrating. Explain what enters and what exits; do not dwell on API syntax.
:::

## Inspect raw output before trusting the parsed label

<div class="object-type">str</div>
<div class="object-view">{
  "id": 3,
  "label": "SUPPORT",
  "evidence": "I want lower rents"
}</div>

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 32px;">The JSON is well formed. The evidence is real. The measurement is still wrong under our codebook.</div>

::: {.notes}
The output is instructor-authored cached material. Ask why valid JSON and verbatim evidence are insufficient validation.
:::

---

## Parsing changes the type—not the truth status

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-7"}
import json

parsed = json.loads(raw_text)
model_label = parsed["label"]

print(type(raw_text))   # str
print(type(parsed))     # dict
```

<div class="semantic-line" style="margin-top: 30px;">A parser can guarantee structure. It cannot guarantee construct validity.</div>

::: {.notes}
Ask students to predict both printed types. Connect “structure” to the role of a schema and “validity” to comparison with the reference/codebook.
:::

## An 83% accuracy rate coexists with a biased estimate

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
<div class="evidence-number">10/12</div>
<div class="evidence-label">labels match the human reference</div>
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 30px;">Both errors convert **conditional** statements into support.</div>

The error mechanism is substantively coherent, not a random sprinkling of mistakes.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
All numbers derive from synthetic course data. Return to the opening question and ask who would now accept the classifier for prevalence estimation.
:::

## Count outcomes by following four mutually exclusive branches

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-10"}
if human_support and model_support:
    counts["tp"] += 1
elif not human_support and model_support:
    counts["fp"] += 1
elif human_support and not model_support:
    counts["fn"] += 1
else:
    counts["tn"] += 1
```

<div class="semantic-line validation" style="margin-top: 26px;">Every record enters exactly one branch. Predict which branch comment 3 enters.</div>

::: {.notes}
Have the less experienced partner explain the Boolean expressions. Comment 3 is human not-support/model-support, hence false positive.
:::

---

## Each metric answers a different question

<div class="metric-row"><strong>Precision</strong><span class="value">.67</span><span>Of predicted support, how much is reference support?</span></div>
<div class="metric-row"><strong>Recall</strong><span class="value">1.00</span><span>Of reference support, how much did the model recover?</span></div>
<div class="metric-row"><strong>F1</strong><span class="value">.80</span><span>How strong is their harmonic balance?</span></div>

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 22px;">High recall does not rescue a prevalence estimate inflated by false positives.</div>

<div class="source-line">Barrie, Argyle, Bisbee et al., 2026 · §10.2.5</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Claim: Balanced metrics such as F1 and direct inspection of the confusion matrix are preferable to agreement alone, especially for rare categories | Source: course chapter §10.2.5 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
Metrics are computed from synthetic data: TP=4, FP=2, FN=0, TN=6.
:::

## The two errors share the same boundary condition

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<div class="label failure">Comment 3</div>

“I want lower rents, **but I cannot support** the proposal unless…”

Model evidence: “I want lower rents”
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
<div class="label failure">Comment 11</div>

“I **could accept** additional housing **if** the city first guarantees…”

Model evidence: “I could accept additional housing”
:::
::::

<div class="semantic-line warning" style="margin-top: 30px;">The model detects favorable language and underweights the condition governing stance.</div>

::: {.notes}
Synthetic course material. Ask whether prompt revision, human adjudication, a new category, or a different inferential target is the best response.
:::

---

## Error inspection can force a theoretical decision

<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Option 1</strong> Keep UNCLEAR and strengthen the conditional-case rule</div>
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Option 2</strong> Add CONDITIONAL as a theoretically meaningful category</div>
<div class="comparison-band"><strong>Option 3</strong> Change the target from explicit support to openness under conditions</div>

<div class="semantic-line validation" style="margin-top: 30px;">Validation is not only model checking. It can refine the measure and the question.</div>

::: {.notes}
Have students choose an option and say what downstream quantity it would produce. There is no universally correct answer; the research question governs.
:::

---

## A defensible workflow stacks several checks

1. **Construct:** labels and boundary cases represent the concept.
2. **Reference:** humans code a held-out, strategically sampled subset.
3. **Performance:** inspect confusion, class metrics, and substantive quantities.
4. **Pattern:** test error by text type, subgroup, period, and theoretical variables.
5. **Dependence:** vary prompt, model/runtime, and collection date.
6. **Inference:** revise the claim or correct downstream estimation.

<div class="source-line">Barrie, Argyle, Bisbee et al., 2026 · Stuhler et al., 2025 · Chae & Davidson, 2026</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Validation principles: held-out human comparison, balanced metrics, non-random error, model/version revalidation, cost/performance comparison | Source: course chapter §10.2.5; https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251336794; https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251325243 | Accessed: 2026-08-18
[/Sources]
:::

2. Calculate precision, recall, and F1 for SUPPORT.
3. Run the supplied checks.
4. Explain why the two false positives matter for the support estimate.
5. Connect the pattern to one required reading in 100–150 words.

<div class="semantic-line" style="margin-top: 34px;">Complete means: prediction · working code · interpreted check · reading-linked claim.</div>

## Revise the claim to match the evidence {.question-slide}

<div class="major-question" style="margin-top: 46px;">
This promptbook produces useful provisional labels—but it does not yet support an unbiased estimate of explicit support.
</div>

<div class="lead" style="margin-top: 48px;">What new evidence would let you strengthen that sentence?</div>

::: {.notes}
Exit record: claim → target → evidence → failure mode → revised claim. Ask students to name one validation sample or design change, not simply “more data.”
:::
